artwork.title: The Death of Sardanapalus
artwork.imageCredit: Photo: Shonagon, 2025, via Wikimedia Commons · Public Domain

lessons.title: A veritable fiasco?

n1.text: A huge red bed slants across the canvas. Around it: a woman held at knifepoint, a man dragging a white horse, gold and jewels heaped on the floor. Beyond, smoke.

voice.speaker: delacroix
voice.text: Before the story, just look. Let the red bed carry your eye from the top left down to the bottom right.

n1b.text: Somewhere in this chaos is Sardanapalus, an ancient king of Assyria. The Salon booklet explained the scene: rebels besiege his palace, and from his bed, on top of an immense pyre, he orders his women and pages killed.

q1.text: Where did Delacroix find this story?

b1a.text: Right king, but Delacroix started from a newer book.

correction.tempting: The old story of Sardanapalus and his pyre is told by the ancient historian Diodorus of Sicily.
correction.truth: Delacroix took it from Lord Byron's play Sardanapalus, published in 1821. Byron himself had drawn on Diodorus.
correction.evidence: Philadelphia Museum of Art: 'inspired by Lord Byron's dramatic poem of 1821'. Moreau-Nélaton (1916) and Charles Rivet (printed 1865): from Byron. Byron's preface and his editor Coleridge: Diodorus.

b1b.text: Yes. Three independent writers name Byron's play of 1821: the Philadelphia Museum of Art, the biographer Étienne Moreau-Nélaton, and Charles Rivet, in an article printed in 1865.

b1c.text: We do know: three writers name the same play.

correction.tempting: Sardanapalus's story has more than one teller, from the ancient historian Diodorus to Lord Byron.
correction.truth: Three independent writers say Delacroix took it from Lord Byron's play Sardanapalus, published in 1821.
correction.evidence: Philadelphia Museum of Art. Étienne Moreau-Nélaton, Delacroix raconté par lui-même (1916). Charles Rivet's article, printed by Achille Piron (1865).

n2.text: Byron's play came out in 1821. Delacroix turned it into a canvas almost four metres high and five wide. How long do you think that took?

q2.text: How long did the big canvas take him?

b2a.text: There was earlier work, but not on this canvas.

correction.tempting: A smaller oil sketch of the whole composition goes back to 1826–1827.
correction.truth: The big canvas itself was painted in the second half of 1827: about six months.
correction.evidence: Louvre record: painted in the second half of 1827. Delacroix, letter of 6 February 1828: 'six months of work' (our translation). Sketch: Louvre record and Robaut (1885).

b2b.text: Yes. The Louvre dates it to the second half of 1827, and Delacroix himself wrote, in February 1828, of 'six months of work' (our translation).

correction.tempting: He had a deadline: the Salon of 1827 opened on 4 November.
correction.truth: He spent about six months on it, the second half of 1827.
correction.evidence: Louvre record: painted in the second half of 1827. Delacroix, letter of 6 February 1828: 'six months of work' (our translation).

n3.text: Six months on a wall of paint. Early biographers saw England in it: Philippe Burty, Maurice Tourneux and Étienne Moreau-Nélaton each linked it to English painting or to his trip to London.

n3b.text: He meant it for the Salon of 1827, the big public art exhibition in Paris. It opened on 4 November 1827.

q3.text: When could Salon visitors first see this picture?

b3a.text: That was the plan, but he missed it.

correction.tempting: It's catalogued as a picture of the Salon of 1827, and that Salon opened on 4 November.
correction.truth: It wasn't ready in time. It went on show only in early February 1828, when the Salon renewed its pictures.
correction.evidence: Moreau-Nélaton (1916): not ready for 4 November. Louvre record: shown from early February 1828. Delacroix, 6 February 1828: the Salon 'reopened this morning' (our translation).

b3b.text: Yes. It wasn't ready in time. The Salon renewed its pictures early in 1828, and this one went on show in early February.

b3c.text: It caused a storm, but it got in.

correction.tempting: Critics hated it, so you might expect the jury to shut it out.
correction.truth: The jury admitted it, and it hung at the Salon from early February 1828.
correction.evidence: Louvre record: admitted by the jury, shown from February 1828. Delacroix, letter of 6 February 1828: his picture is 'placed the best in the world' (our translation).

n4.text: It came so late that the booklet lists it only in a second supplement. Now Paris could judge it.

q4.text: How did the critics take it?

correction.tempting: Today it hangs among the Louvre's great Romantic pictures, in the Salle Mollien.
correction.truth: In 1828 the reviews were harsh. The critic Augustin Jal wrote that in this picture 'the beauties do not exist' (our translation).
correction.evidence: Jal, Salon review, 1828. Philadelphia Museum of Art: it 'received harsh criticism'. Louvre: judged shocking at the time.

b4b.text: Yes. The Philadelphia Museum of Art says it 'received harsh criticism'. The critic Augustin Jal went further: in this picture, 'the beauties do not exist' (our translation).

correction.tempting: It arrived late, tucked into a supplement of the booklet.
correction.truth: Critics attacked it. The Louvre says it was judged shocking at the time; Jal wrote that 'the beauties do not exist' (our translation).
correction.evidence: Louvre, 2023 activity report. Augustin Jal, Salon review, 1828. Philadelphia Museum of Art: 'harsh criticism'.

n5.text: In March 1828, Delacroix wrote to Charles Soulier about the Salon.

voice.speaker: delacroix
voice.text: They will end by persuading me that I have made a veritable fiasco … that the death of Sardanapalus is the death of the Romantics — since romantics there are.
voice.cite: Letter to Charles Soulier, 11 March 1828 (English translation: Dorothy Bussy, 1907)

n5b.text: The State had bought his earlier big picture, the Massacre at Chios, straight away. What would happen to this one?

q5.text: What happened to the picture after the Salon?

correction.tempting: The State had bought his Massacre at Chios at once.
correction.truth: No buyer came. Delacroix kept it in his studio until 1846.
correction.evidence: Louvre record: he failed to sell it. Tourneux (1902): it went back to his studio and stayed a long time. Philadelphia Museum of Art: sold in 1846.

b5b.text: Yes. Nobody bought it. Delacroix kept it in his studio until 1846, when the collector Daniel Wilson finally bought it.

b5c.text: A collector came, but much later.

correction.tempting: A private collector, Daniel Wilson, did buy it from Delacroix.
correction.truth: But only in 1846. Until then it stayed, unsold, in Delacroix's studio.
correction.evidence: Louvre record: sold to Daniel Wilson in 1846. Editors of his Journal (1893): Wilson bought it. Tourneux (1902): it stayed in his studio a long time.

n6.text: Years later, in notes printed after his death, he looked back on the time after this Salon.

voice.speaker: delacroix
voice.text: You may judge what such enforced idleness meant for me … at a moment when I felt myself capable of covering a whole town with my paintings.
voice.cite: His notes, printed by Piron, 1865 (English translation: Dorothy Bussy, 1907)

n6b.text: He didn't drop the subject: in 1844 he painted a small replica, now in Philadelphia. And before the big canvas, he had made studies for it.

q6.text: Delacroix's will left the painter Maréchal several studies for it. What were they?

b6a.text: Yes: 'several pastel studies for Sardanapalus', says the will (our translation). One of them, a study of a slipper, is now in the Louvre.

b6b.text: It exists, but it went elsewhere.

correction.tempting: Delacroix did make a smaller oil sketch of the whole composition.
correction.truth: The will left Maréchal pastel studies. The oil sketch went to the Rivet family, and it is in the Louvre now too.
correction.evidence: Delacroix's will, printed by Burty (1878). Louvre records of the sketch and of a pastel bequeathed to Maréchal. Robaut (1885): sketch owned by the baronne Rivet.

b6c.text: He had parted with that long before.

correction.tempting: He had kept the big canvas in his studio for years.
correction.truth: He sold it to Daniel Wilson in 1846. The will left Maréchal 'several pastel studies' for it (our translation).
correction.evidence: Louvre record and Philadelphia Museum of Art: sold in 1846. Delacroix's will, printed by Burty (1878).

n7.text: So: Byron's play, six months of work, a late arrival, harsh reviews, years unsold. Today it hangs in Room 700, the Salle Mollien. Let the red bed lead your eye, and judge for yourself.

lessons.takeaway: Delacroix turned Byron's play into six months of work that arrived late at the Salon, was savaged in 1828 and stayed unsold in his studio until 1846.
